cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and the thing you built is holding.
cells.act: hold space for what someone feels without fixing it
cells.ask: Sit with someone while they are upset for five minutes — just be there, no fix, no reason.
cells.core:
What you build under your hands holds. Not because you clutch it, but because you know what it costs and pay it without complaint. That's the strength under the care: you can set a finished thing down, and pick it back up when someone needs it.

That steadiness leaves room for whoever else is present. This week, when someone near you is upset, stay with what they feel for a few minutes instead of solving it. It'll feel unfinished. That's what being near someone without merging looks like: two people in the same rain, neither one drowned. You'll know it worked when they keep talking.
cells.sheetLine: You build what holds, and you can put it down.
cells.place: in the tending of what is still growing

cells.tense: You are carrying what is still growing toward a future you keep rehearsing.
cells.act: weigh what it costs them against what it gives
cells.ask: Look at the push you keep making at someone close, ask what it costs them, and hold off a week.
cells.core:
Seeds under your care get measured against the orchard. The measuring has crowded out the waiting, and today's growth keeps losing to a season that hasn't come. The work itself is good. The pace is borrowed. Your grip moves faster than the thing can grow, and it shows in how often you check.

There's a fairer way to hold it. Look at the push you keep making — at a person, a plan, a pace — and ask honestly what your forcing costs them. Then leave it alone for a week. Not forever — a week. What you're building will still be there, and you'll find out whether the hurry was the work's or yours. Most of it was yours. The seed doesn't need you to be the season.
cells.sheetLine: You're measuring the harvest, and it's edged out the waiting.
cells.place: in the tending of what is still growing

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door the building has already grown past.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Mark done what already finished — close the file, hand it off, box it up — and turn back to what's still green.
cells.core:
Things under your care got tended long past the point where tending helped. Your hands are still working a shape that finished — rearranging it, protecting it — while the ground under it has moved on. The work you're doing is steady and careful, and it's aimed at something the room no longer needs.

There's an older, lighter way to hold a duty: know when to set it down. Mark done what already finished — close the file, hand it off, box it up — then turn back to what's still green. Not abandoned — completed. What's growing doesn't need a guard on the old growth, and your hands were waiting for the word.
cells.sheetLine: You're guarding a finished thing. Let it be finished.
cells.place: in the tending of what is still growing

cells.tense: You are writing in a room you keep calling someone else's.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Pick up a fresh thing this week because something in you sparked, not because anyone asked.
cells.core:
Something young is under your hand, and the hand is steady while the credit goes elsewhere. You know the light, the water, the pace — and when anything comes up healthy, it gets chalked up to luck. You are the one who made the conditions. In a room where your hand is plainly the one writing, another name keeps ending up on the page.

A cleaner way to see it: start something that's yours. Pick up a fresh thing this week — a page, a plan, a plant — because something in you sparked, not because it was needed. Nothing has to come of it. You'll feel the difference between carrying and making. What you cultivate reaches its own shine, and the shine belongs to whoever did the cultivating. That's you. The room already has your name on it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the light on and let it be called luck.
cells.place: in the tending of what is still growing

attempts.check: My draft's weakest claim is that 'the person can name what they are growing' in the Too Little cell — the record says the capacity is withdrawn, not that they can name it; I have narrowed it to not being able to point at it yet, not to not knowing. A reader could reasonably say 'I never knew what I was building' and still find the release offer usable, since it asks them to stop holding a shared thing, not to name it. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'You can name what you are growing,' which I have replaced with a plainer beat about not tightening what can't be pointed at yet.
